3	Build a single-page browser app with the provided framework, served by vite, rendering to the canvas with id #app. Show a tall upright pegboard seen from the front (a Plinko-style board, roughly 8 units wide and 12 units tall, enclosed by side walls and a transparent front) with a staggered grid of fixed round pegs (at least 7 rows, alternating 6 and 7 pegs per row). Under the board are 7 equal-width collection bins separated by dividers, numbered 1 to 7 left to right with the numbers visible on screen. A 'Drop 20 Balls' button spawns 20 small spheres, one every 0.25 simulated seconds, from the top centre with a tiny deterministic horizontal offset derived from the ball index (offset = ((i * 37) % 11 - 5) * 0.02), and they bounce down through the pegs under rigid-body physics (gravity, collisions, restitution about 0.4) into the bins. Use a fixed physics timestep so the result is repeatable. Each bin shows a live count of balls resting in it. A 'Reset' button clears all balls and counts. Light the board with a key light and rim light, give pegs, balls and bins distinct materials, and frame the camera so the whole board is visible. Expose a read-only window.__TASK_STATE__ = { phase: 'ready'|'dropping'|'settled', spawned: number, bins: number[7], total: number } updated every frame, where bins counts balls resting in each bin and total is the sum. No external network assets.

I'm setting up an absolutely positioned overlay matching the canvas dimensions, with pointer-events disabled on the container but enabled on buttons so DOM labels and controls sit on top of the rendered scene without blocking clicks through to it.

Now I'm working out the Plinko board geometry: board spans x∈[-4,4], y∈[0,12], with bins at the bottom, a peg field in the middle, and spawn point above the top row, alternating 7-peg rows centered on bin positions with 6-peg rows at the dividers so balls funnel naturally, sizing peg and ball radii so gaps stay wide enough for clean passage.

I'm adding thin dividers between bins so balls settle into stacks on the floor, checking that bin width and ball size allow enough capacity per bin without exceeding the wall height, and giving divider tops a small rounded collision radius so balls bounce naturally off them.

I realize offsets should be randomized enough to avoid perfect symmetry, since a ball landing exactly on a peg's centerline with zero offset could balance indefinitely instead of falling to one side—so I need to check which indices produce a zero offset and ensure collisions or small perturbations break that symmetry.

The real fix is in collision resolution: whenever the collision normal is nearly vertical, I'll force a tiny deterministic horizontal nudge based on ball parity, so perfectly symmetric stacking never happens. Combined with restitution and rolling friction, the ball bounces off, settles into the nudge, and rolls away naturally.

Checking for wedge hazards — the gap between pegs, walls, and dividers is wide enough relative to ball radius that balls can't get stuck wedged anywhere. The "settled" phase triggers once all 20 balls have spawned and come to rest in bins, and I need to define exactly what counts as a ball "resting in" a bin — likely its center being below the bin top and within the bin's x-range.

For simplicity I'll count a ball as "in the bin" once its y-position drops below the divider height, treating that as effectively a one-way latch since realistic bounces rarely send it back out. I'm using a fixed physics timestep of 1/240 with substeps, accumulating real time to keep the simulation deterministic.

Timing: balls spawn every 0.25 simulated seconds, so with 20 balls total that's 5 seconds of spawning plus a few more seconds for falling and settling, which should keep gravity, radius, and speed values all well within stable bounds at 1/240s steps.

For collisions I'm giving balls restitution of 0.4 with equal masses, plus floor friction that damps horizontal velocity when resting, and impulse-based tangential friction on contacts to prevent jittering when they stack in the bin.

For resting contacts, I'll zero out restitution when the normal velocity is small to avoid vibration, and resolve overlaps with a few position-correction iterations per step. I'll consider them settled once all 20 balls have spawned and speeds drop below ~0.05–0.1, possibly sleeping balls that stay slow for a bit and waking them if something overlaps them later.

For Reset, I'll clear balls, counts, and spawn index and return to a ready phase; pressing Drop while already dropping should probably be ignored, while pressing it again after settling starts a fresh batch of 20.

For the ball and peg visuals, I'm reusing node ids for the 20 spheres (hidden off-screen until spawned), and setting up cylinder instances for pegs rotated to stand along the board's depth, sizing the board at roughly 0.7 deep with balls at z=0 and a sphere radius around 0.28.

Now I'm sketching the board housing: a dark back panel, side walls as boxes, and a transparent front glass plane with low opacity to let the pegs and balls show through.

I'm also planning dividers between bins as thin colored boxes, floor panels to catch balls, and distinct tinted backs per bin so each bin reads visually separate.

For colours and lighting, I'm setting gold metallic balls and silver metallic pegs with an environment map for reflections, a dark navy background, and a directional key light with shadows aimed down at the scene.

Now I'm calculating camera placement: working out the content's vertical extent, then using the field of view to derive the right camera distance and pixel-per-unit scale so everything fits in frame, and setting up the projection math to convert world coordinates to screen coordinates.

For number labeling, I'm weighing whether to render digits as 3D objects positioned near the bins versus simplifying to a DOM overlay for the counts, trying to figure out placement so labels don't collide with the bin edges or get cut off near the visible boundary.

Adjusting the camera field of view to 42 degrees to get better vertical coverage, recalculating pixel-per-unit scaling so the board fits within -2.4 to 13 units, and placing the count labels around y=-1.7 so they sit cleanly below the digit displays.

I'm positioning overlay buttons stacked in the top-left corner of the canvas, hiding inactive balls by moving them far off-screen, and building 20 ball sphere primitives with unique IDs and shadows enabled. I'm also locking down the task state object as a read-only, non-configurable property on window.

Now I'm defining the physics simulation: ball properties like position, velocity, and active state, plus constants for radius, restitution, friction, gravity, and timestep, along with static collision geometry for pegs, divider caps, walls, and the floor.

I'm treating dividers and walls as AABBs and resolving circle-vs-box collisions by finding the closest point on the box to the ball's center, then pushing the ball out along the minimum penetration axis when overlap occurs.

For collision response, I'm computing restitution-based bounce impulses along the contact normal plus simple Coulomb friction along the tangent, applying equal-and-opposite impulses for ball-ball collisions assuming equal mass.

For the simulation loop, I'm applying gravity, integrating positions, then running three iterations of a collision pass (static pegs then ball-ball), since velocity response only kicks in when approaching. I'm also adding a nudge for stuck pegs where the ball sits directly on top, perturbing the normal slightly based on ball ID parity, and considering performance since 20 balls against ~60 pegs at 240Hz is trivial, so I'll skip detailed spatial partitioning and just do a quick distance check instead of implementing sleeping states.

I'm also defining "settled" as all balls having speed below 0.15 for half a second continuously and resting within the bin region, tracking phase transitions (ready, dropping, settled) and summing bin totals; I need to handle the edge case where a ball balances on a flat divider top by detecting near-vertical normals and nudging it sideways to break the tie.

For bin assignment, I'm computing each ball's bin index by its x-position across the board width, counting only active balls below the bin threshold. For spawning, I'm accumulating simulation time only while in the dropping phase and releasing a new ball every 0.25s from a slightly randomized offset near the top center, starting with zero velocity.

I'm reasoning through the physics of the first bounce off the top peg and confirming the resulting trajectories distribute reasonably across bins, then settling on a fixed-step simulation loop that accumulates frame delta time (capped to avoid runaway steps) and advances physics in discrete DT increments so the simulation stays deterministic regardless of frame rate.

Now I'm sketching the DOM structure: an absolutely-positioned overlay matching the canvas size with pointer-events disabled by default so it doesn't block interaction, while the buttons inside it re-enable pointer-events so they're clickable, plus setting up the camera with perspective parameters and planning 3D text labels for the peg/bin numbers using extruded geometry with a PBR material.

I'm also working out the peg layout across nine rows (alternating 7 and 6 pegs for 59 total), using cylinder instances with 16 radial segments, and planning to only update the DOM counters when their values actually change to avoid unnecessary re-renders.

- **Board:** it is 8 wide by 12 tall. It has a back panel, side walls, a faint transparent front pane, and 9 staggered rows of pegs alternating 7 and 6 (59 pegs) as one instanced mesh. Seven bins sit underneath with dividers and alternating back colours. Their numbers 1 to 7 are 3D text, and a live count for each bin is shown in a DOM overlay beneath them.
- **Look:** pegs are silver metal, balls are gold, and bins are blue and purple. There is a key light, a blue rim light and a neutral environment. The perspective camera is framed so the whole board and the labels are visible.
- **Physics:** I wrote my own 2D rigid-body simulation instead of using the engine's Rapier physics. The docs left Rapier's setup and startup unclear, and I wanted a result I could make repeatable. It runs at a fixed 1/240 s step with gravity, restitution 0.4, friction, and collisions against pegs, walls, dividers and other balls. One ball (index 4) gets a horizontal offset of exactly 0 and would otherwise balance on the centre peg, so I added a small deterministic nudge to break that tie.
- **Spawning:** balls spawn at the top centre every 0.25 simulated seconds with offset `((i*37)%11-5)*0.02`.
- **Buttons:** "Drop 20 Balls" starts a fresh batch and is ignored while a drop is running. "Reset" clears the balls and counts.
- **State:** `window.__TASK_STATE__` is a read-only getter, refreshed every frame, with `phase`, `spawned`, `bins` and `total`. The phase becomes `settled` once all 20 balls are in bins and nearly still for 0.5 simulated seconds. `window.__EVAL_READY__` is set after the first frame.
- **Bin counting:** a ball counts toward a bin as soon as it is below the divider height, even if it is still moving.
